topics.title: Role evolution and unwritten responsibilities
topics.rationale: No role or department is recorded; understanding what they actually did day-to-day reveals gaps in the formal org chart.
seed_questions: What was your job title on paper, and what did you actually spend most of your time doing?
Which tasks fell to you that were never in any job description?
Who depended on your decisions or approvals that wouldn't show up in an org chart?

topics.title: Key equipment and systems they owned
topics.rationale: No equipment is linked to this profile; we need them to name the assets they knew intimately.
seed_questions: Which pumps, compressors, vessels, or control loops did you consider 'yours'?
If you got a call at 2 a.m., which equipment tag was most likely the reason?
Are there any pieces of equipment you nursed along that nobody else really understands?

topics.title: Chronic equipment issues and workarounds
topics.rationale: Undocumented failure patterns and field fixes are the highest-value knowledge at risk of walking out the door.
seed_questions: Which piece of equipment failed repeatedly in ways the work orders never fully captured?
What temporary fixes became permanent and why was a proper repair never done?
Are there any vibration, temperature, or sound signatures you learned to recognize as early warnings?

topics.title: Unfinished projects and half-done modifications
topics.rationale: Projects they touched may be in limbo with tribal knowledge about why they stalled or what remains.
seed_questions: Which projects did you start or contribute to that never got formally closed out?
Are there any modifications or bypasses installed that were meant to be temporary but are still in place?
What project documentation exists but is misleading because the actual installed configuration is different?

topics.title: Vendor and contractor relationship intelligence
topics.rationale: Knowing which vendor reps to trust, who to avoid, and unwritten service history saves months of trial and error.
seed_questions: Which equipment vendors or local reps actually understood our plant and which ones gave us bad advice?
Are there any third-party contractors or specialists you always called for certain jobs because internal crews couldn't handle it?
What verbal agreements or understandings exist with suppliers that aren't in any contract?

topics.title: Critical operating procedures that differ from the written SOP
topics.rationale: Operators often develop safer or more effective methods that never make it back into the controlled documents.
seed_questions: Which standard operating procedure did you never follow exactly as written, and why?
Are there any startup or shutdown sequences where the real-world order of steps is different from the manual?
What alarms or trips do people routinely suppress or work around, and what is the safe way to do it?

topics.title: Process safety and near-miss memory
topics.rationale: Near-misses and weak points in safety barriers are rarely documented with the richness of someone who was there.
seed_questions: What was the closest you ever came to a serious process safety event that never made it into an incident report?
Which safety interlocks or relief systems have you seen challenged or bypassed?
Are there any operating envelopes (pressure, temperature, level) where you know the stated limits are wrong or optimistic?

topics.title: Tuning parameters and control loop folklore
topics.rationale: PID tuning values, DCS logic quirks, and controller settings often live only in the minds of the people who tweaked them.
seed_questions: Which control loops have tuning parameters you set by feel and never documented?
Are there any DCS or PLC logic sequences that have 'features' only you know how to work around?
What setpoints or ramp rates do you use that differ from the official recipe or control narrative?

topics.title: Maintenance history gaps and repeat failure patterns
topics.rationale: CMMS data often misses the 'why' behind repeat failures; the retiree knows which fixes never stuck.
seed_questions: Which equipment had the same failure mode repaired multiple times without ever addressing the root cause?
Are there any spare parts that are supposed to fit but actually require field modification?
What preventive maintenance tasks on the schedule are a waste of time, and what should replace them?

topics.title: Shift handover and abnormal situation management
topics.rationale: How they managed transitions and abnormal ops contains patterns a successor needs to replicate.
seed_questions: What information did you always make sure to pass on during shift handover that never fit in the logbook?
When the plant was in an upset condition, what was your personal mental checklist that isn't written anywhere?
What is the one situation you hope your successor never faces, and what should they do if it happens?

topics.title: Successor readiness and open risks
topics.rationale: Direct advice to the successor and a frank assessment of lurking risks is the core purpose of the exit interview.
seed_questions: What are the top three things your replacement needs to learn in the first month that they won't find in any file?
What is the biggest operational risk you see on the horizon that management isn't paying enough attention to?
If you could leave one handwritten note taped inside a control panel for the next person, what would it say?

topics.title: Plant-wide gotchas and unwritten rules
topics.rationale: Every plant has quirks—certain valves that stick, instruments that lie in specific weather, combinations to avoid.
seed_questions: What are the 'never do this' rules that everyone who has been here a while knows but a new person wouldn't?
Are there any instrument readings that you know to distrust under certain conditions?
What seasonal or weather-related behaviors of the plant should someone watch for?

topics.title: Training and knowledge transfer gaps they experienced
topics.rationale: Their own experience of being trained reveals systemic weaknesses in how the plant passes on knowledge.
seed_questions: When you started in this role, what did nobody teach you that you had to learn the hard way?
What training materials or programs exist but are outdated or misleading?
Who else in the plant holds pieces of knowledge that really belong to your role?

transcript.text: Currently, the DOS second, let's say,

Srinjoy, I think you were about to say something — "the DOS second.. ." — go ahead and finish that thought if you'd like. But let me take a step back first. I'm here because you're retiring, and there's knowledge in your head that nobody else has — the kind of thing that isn't in any manual or handover document. That's what I want to capture today.

So let me start with this: what's your actual role here at the plant, and if you had to pick one thing you'd most want your successor to know, what would it be?
Thank you, this has been genuinely valuable. I am writing up your handover document now.
